extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners and patent applicants (biotechnology and general patent practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and drafting patent applications under the ARIPO/Harare Protocol, with emphasis on biotechnological subject-matter, exceptions to patentability, industrial application, and prior art (including internet disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material isolated or produced by technical process is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological material which is isolated from its natural environment or produced by means of a technical process is patentable even if it previously occurred in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biological material may be considered patentable even if it already occurs in nature; however the human body at various stages and the simple discovery of one of its elements (including sequence or partial sequence of a gene) cannot constitute patentable inventions. The industrial application of a sequence or partial sequence must be disclosed in the patent application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human body elements and gene sequences exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The human body, at the various stages of its formation and development, and the simple discovery of one of its elements, including the sequence or partial sequence of a gene, cannot constitute patentable inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination of gene sequence applications should be subject to the same criteria of patentability as other technologies, and the industrial application of a sequence or partial sequence must be disclosed in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plants or animals patentable when not confined to a particular variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants or animals are patentable provided that the technical feasibility of the invention is not confined to a particular plant or animal variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that does not individually claim specific plant varieties is not excluded even though it may embrace plant varieties; subject-matter of a claim covering but not identifying plant varieties is not a claim to a variety or varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim covering plant varieties without identification is not a variety claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim wherein specific plant varieties are not individually claimed is not excluded from patentability even though it may embrace plant varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of identification of a specific plant variety in a product claim, the claimed subject-matter is neither limited nor directed to a variety or varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microbiological process definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Microbiological process" means any process involving or performed upon or resulting in microbiological material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted to cover processes performed upon microbiological material, processes resulting in such material (e.g. by genetic engineering), and processes including both microbiological and non-microbiological steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of microbiological processes may be patented per se
rubrics_metrics.description: The product of a microbiological process may also be patentable per se (product claim). Propagation of the microorganism itself is to be construed as a microbiological process; consequently the microorganism can be protected per se as a product obtained by a microbiological process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term microorganism includes bacteria, plasmids, viruses, unicellular fungi (including yeasts), algae, protozoa and human/animal/plant cells. However, product claims for plant or animal varieties cannot be allowed even if produced by a microbiological process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability requirement for microbiological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of microbiological processes, particular regard should be had to the requirement of repeatability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatability is assured by the possibility of taking samples and by deposits under Rule 6bis.2; there is thus no need to indicate another process for production of the biological material where deposit-based repeatability is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception: inventions contrary to "ordre public" or morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Any invention the commercial exploitation of which would be contrary to "ordre public" or morality is specifically excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a fair test: consider whether it is probable that the public in general would regard the invention as so abhorrent that grant of patent rights would be inconceivable. Mere possibility of abuse is not sufficient if the invention can be exploited in non-offensive ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited matter is not automatically excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploitation is not to be deemed contrary to "ordre public" or morality merely because it is prohibited by law or regulation in some or all Contracting States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product could still be manufactured under an ARIPO patent for export to States in which its use is not prohibited; prohibition by law in some states alone does not justify exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive and non-offensive use balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention has both an offensive and a non-offensive use, refusal of a patent may be unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a safe-opening process usable by burglars (offensive) but also by locksmiths (non-offensive) — in such a case, no objection arises. If the application explicitly references an offensive use, deletion of that reference should be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARIPO not to consider economic effects in exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ARIPO has not been vested with the task of taking into account the economic effects of the grant of patents and of restricting patentable subject-matter accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard for an exception is whether commercial exploitation is contrary to "ordre public" or morality, not economic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnological exclusions under Rule 7bis.3 (illustrative list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 7bis.3 ARIPO patents are not to be granted in respect of biotechnological inventions which concern certain listed items (illustrative and non-exhaustive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed exceptions include: (i) processes for cloning human beings; (ii) processes for modifying the germ line genetic identity of human beings; (iii) uses of human embryos for industrial or commercial purposes (does not affect therapeutic/diagnostic uses useful to the embryo); (iv) processes for modifying genetic identity of animals likely to cause them suffering without substantial medical benefit and animals resulting from such processes; exclusion also of processes to produce chimeras from germ cells or totipotent cells of humans and animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant or animal varieties and essentially biological processes exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 7bis.3 includes 'plant or animal varieties or essentially biological processes for the production of plants or animals' among exceptions to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process for the production of a plant variety is not a priori excluded merely because resulting product may constitute a plant variety; an 'essentially biological' process consists entirely of natural phenomena such as crossing or selection and is unpatentable. Processes involving technical steps (e.g. treating a plant with growth-stimulating substance or radiation, or soil treatment by technical means) are not essentially biological and may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for treatment by surgery, therapy and diagnostic methods exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: ARIPO patents are not to be granted in respect of 'methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practiced on the human or animal body'; this provision does not apply to products, in particular substances or compositions, for use in any of these methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic instruments or apparatuses for use in such methods may be patented. Manufacturing steps outside the body that require no surgical intervention are patentable; but a manufacturing method requiring a surgical step (e.g. taking measurements on patient) would be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: First medical use and subsequent medical uses (Swiss-type claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A known substance or composition may be patented for use in surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic methods if that use was not previously disclosed ('first medical use'); claims in 'Swiss-type' form are allowable for first and subsequent such applications if new and inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form of claim: 'Substance or composition X' followed by indication of the use (e.g. '... for use as a medicament'). A known substance may be patented for second or further uses provided the use is novel and inventive; product claims for medical uses must still satisfy other patentability requirements, especially inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited claim form for therapeutic use
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim in the form 'Use of substance or composition X for the treatment of disease Y...' will be regarded as relating to a method for treatment explicitly excluded from patentability and therefore will not be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should use allowable claim formats such as Swiss-type claims ('for the manufacture of a medicament for therapeutic application Z') for patentable medical use claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of multiple distinct therapeutic uses in one application
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application discloses for the first time a number of distinct surgical, therapeutic or diagnostic uses for a known substance, normally independent claims each directed to the substance for one of the various uses may be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is subject to the requirement that the multiple uses form a single general inventive concept; lack of unity of invention should not be raised as a general rule in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic method definition (four phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a claim is directed to a diagnostic method it must include method steps relating to all of the following phases: (i) the examination phase (collection of data); (ii) comparison of data with standard values; (iii) finding of any significant deviation (a symptom); (iv) attribution of the deviation to a particular clinical picture (deductive medical/veterinary decision phase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these essential phases are missing and are essential for the invention, they must be included in the independent claim. Some steps (e.g. comparison implying finding) may be implicit; phase (iv) is normally an intellectual exercise and not technical unless a device reaches diagnostic conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Practiced on the human or animal body" criterion for diagnostic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to fulfill the 'practiced on the human or animal body' criterion, each technical method step relating to phases (i) to (iii) must be performed on a human or animal body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each technical method step, ascertain whether an interaction with the human or animal body takes place; direct physical contact is not required and presence of a medical practitioner is not necessary. If these criteria are met, the claim defines a diagnostic method practiced on the body and an objection will be raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods merely obtaining information are not excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for merely obtaining information (data, physical quantities) from the living human or animal body (e.g. X-ray, NMR, blood pressure measurements) are not excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between purely information-obtaining steps and methods that include the decision/therapeutic phases excluded under Rule 7bis.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exceptions to avoid over-extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of exceptions (e.g. surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic) should avoid the exceptions going beyond their proper limits; intention is to free non-commercial and non-industrial medical and veterinary activities from restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exceptions are confined to methods for treatment by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practiced on the body; other technical methods related to live human or animal treatment or measurement may be patentable if technical rather than essentially biological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention shall be considered as susceptible of industrial application if it can be made or used in any kind of industry, including agriculture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry is broad and includes any physical activity of 'technical character'. The description should indicate how the invention is susceptible of industrial application where not self-evident. Inventions that are alleged to operate contrary to well-established physical laws (e.g. perpetual motion) are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of testing considered industrially applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of testing generally should be regarded as inventions susceptible of industrial application and therefore patentable if the test is applicable to improvement or control of a product, apparatus or process which is itself susceptible of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of test animals for industrial testing (e.g. pyrogenetic/allergic effects, pollution phenomena) would be patentable under this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial application does not override other exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Susceptibility of industrial application is not a requirement that overrides other exclusions (e.g. administrative methods excluded under paragraph 3.3.4.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims need not be restricted to industrial applications, but industrial applicability alone does not make otherwise excluded subject-matter patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences and partial sequences: industrial application must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: In relation to sequences and partial sequences of genes, the industrial application of a sequence or a partial sequence must be disclosed in the patent application; a mere nucleic acid sequence without indication of a function is not a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sequence is used to produce a protein or part of a protein, specify which protein/part and what function it performs; alternatively indicate another function (e.g. transcription promoter activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art (novelty) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is 'considered to be new if it does not form part of the state of the art'. The 'state of the art' is everything made available to the public by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way, before the date of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no restrictions as to geographical location, language or manner of disclosure; documents are regarded as publicly available if members of the public could gain knowledge of the content and there was no bar of confidentiality. Examiner should investigate doubtful cases if applicant raises sound reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures form part of the state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of principle, disclosures on the internet form part of the state of the art according to Section 3(10)(c). Information disclosed on the internet is considered publicly available as of the date it was publicly posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet sites often contain highly relevant technical information including online manuals/tutorials. For valid patent practice it is often crucial to cite publications obtainable only from internet websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing publication date for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a publication date requires assessing whether a given date is correctly indicated and whether content was indeed available to the public as of that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet nature makes dating difficult (no timestamps, updates, lack of archives). Neither password protection nor payment prevents a web page from forming part of the state of the art if it is in principle available without confidentiality. Dates can be accepted unless specific indications to the contrary exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When an internet document is cited against an application or patent, the same facts must be established as for other evidence, evaluated under the principle of 'free evaluation of evidence' and using the balance of probabilities standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof beyond reasonable doubt is not required; many internet disclosures contain explicit publication dates generally considered reliable and accepted at face value. Circumstantial evidence may be required to establish or confirm dates; examiner must be convinced on balance of probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof initially with examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: When raising objections, the burden of proof lies initially with the examiner. Objections must be reasoned and substantiated showing that on the balance of probabilities the objection is well-founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If substantiated, the burden shifts to the applicant to prove otherwise. Examiners should consider applicants' reasons if they contest publication dates and may seek further evidence if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability hierarchy for internet sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain internet sources have differing degrees of reliability; online technical journals and 'print-equivalent' publications are generally highly reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical journals from scientific publishers have reliability similar to paper journals. Other reliable sources include newspapers, periodicals, academic institutions, international organizations, public organizations, and standardization bodies. Eprint archives (e.g. arXiv) and other repositories may be used but may be the only disclosure in some cases; pre-published manuscripts should be treated as separate disclosures with their own dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner may request exact publication date when vague
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a given publication date of an online journal is too vague (e.g. only month/year) and the latest possible date is too late, the examiner may request the exact publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request may be made via publisher contact forms or via the ARIPO library; examiner should use judgment whether to spend time at search stage to find further evidence supporting a publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's unsupported generic challenges carry little weight
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant refutes the publication date of an internet disclosure with no reasoning or merely generic statements about internet reliability, such argument will be given minimal weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should provide reasons or evidence to challenge publication dates; otherwise examiner's assumption stands.
